In brief

A "throw-away," according to the OED, is "a printed sheet or work not intended for preservation after it has been read." Synonyms include handbill, handout, leaflet, broadside, broadsheet, flyer, and circular, but the word Joyce chooses uniquely captures the evanescent quality of this sort of publication—its inevitable destiny of becoming trash. He gets plenty of comic and symbolic mileage out of his linguistic find, tying the trashy circular to two promising nobodies: a dark horse and an ancient Jew.

At more length

Mild comedy attends the introduction of the word at the beginning of Lestrygonians. Several paragraphs after a religious proselytizer has "placed a throwaway in a hand of Mr Bloom," announcing that Elijah is coming to Dublin, he reaches the O'Connell Bridge and wonders whether the hungry seagulls swooping over the water might be fooled by a piece of paper: "He threw down among them a crumpled paper ball. Elijah thirtytwo feet per sec is com. Not a bit. The ball bobbed unheeded on the wake of swells, floated under by the bridgepiers. Not such damn fools." Throwaways are meant to be thrown away, and in this case not even the birds are interested. Much later, in Ithaca, Bloom will recall the time "when a dark man had placed in his hand a throwaway (subsequently thrown away), advertising Elijah, restorer of the church in Zion."

He also thinks there of another association bound up in the word, "preindicative of the result of the Gold Cup flat handicap." This second association begins still earlier in the novel. Even though the word "throwaway" is first heard in Lestrygonians, an identical play on its meaning has already occurred in Lotus Eaters when Bantam Lyons asks Bloom if he can take a peek at his newspaper to learn about a horse running in the Gold Cup. He hears Bloom say, "You can keep it. [...] I was just going to throw it away. [...] I say you can keep it [...] I was going to throw it away that moment." Thinking that he has received a covert tip on the likely outcome of the race, Lyons hastily thanks his benefactor and rushes off to throw away his money on a long shot.

Bloom's words are a reminder that newspapers too are publications designed to be discarded after reading. When he eats dinner in the Ormond restaurant he still has the paper, but it is gone by Ithaca, which comically repeats the comical formulation heard moments earlier, noting that Lyons "perused and restituted the copy of the current issue of the Freeman's Journal and National Press which he had been about to throw away (subsequently thrown away)."

In fact Lyons would not have thrown away his money betting on Throwaway. The horse of that name wins the Gold Cup by a length and pays 20-to-1. But Lenehan tells his friends in Barney Kiernan's that he convinced Lyons to back a different horse. Having heard who gave Lyons the tip on Throwaway, he also proclaims in Cyclops that Bloom is "the only man in Dublin has it. A dark horse"—thereby subjecting Bloom, who never bets on horses, to rancorous misunderstanding. His words make others in the bar suppose that Bloom is suddenly rich, and Joe Hynes's response, "He's a bloody dark horse himself," encourages readers' suspicions that he is a loser in life's race, a kind of dark horse that Molly is contemptuously discarding. In Ithaca he imagines himself divorced, homeless, and penniless, a "sandwichman, distributor of throwaways, nocturnal vagrant."

But by the end of Penelope Molly has not resolved to be done with Bloom and is wondering whether she can resuscitate her marriage. Circe imagines "A dark horse, riderless," bolting past "the winningpost" ahead of a field of thoroughbreds. And the Jewish prophet, spotted three times in Wandering Rocks floating down the Liffey as "A skiff, a crumpled throwaway, Elijah is coming," returns in glory at the end of Cyclops in the person of Leopold Bloom ascending to heaven "like a shot off a shovel." Readers will be tempted to draw conclusions from these developments. Jesus was right—the last shall be first? Outcasts have hidden strengths? One person's trash is another's treasure? Whatever the moral may be, it does seem that things thrown away have an uncanny knack for turning up again.

John Hunt 2026
